summary.text: Let \(d=D(n)\) and split \(d=ge\), where \(g\) contains the factors supported on \(2,5\) and \(\gcd(e,10)=1\); from \(n\equiv d\pmod 9\), a linear congruence and Euler’s theorem allow decimal digits of total sum \(n\) to be arranged into a number \(C\) divisible by \(e\). Then \(k=10^dC\) satisfies \(D(k)=n\) and \(d\mid k\), while \(k\ne n\) because a positive multiple of \(10\) has digit sum strictly smaller than itself, so \(k\) is the required partner.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(r)\) denote the sum of the ordinary base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(r\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive Harshad amicable partner distinct from itself. It will then follow immediately that the least such partner exists and is nonzero.

We will use the following elementary facts about decimal digits.

1. For every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
D(r)\le r.
\]
Indeed, if \(r=10q+s\), where \(0\le s<10\), then \(D(r)=D(q)+s\). Induction on the number of digits gives \(D(q)\le q\), and hence
\[
D(r)\le q+s\le 10q+s=r.
\]
If \(r>0\), then at least one decimal digit of \(r\) is nonzero, so \(D(r)>0\).

2. Decimal digit sums preserve residue modulo \(9\):
\[
D(r)\equiv r\pmod 9.
\]
This follows because every power of \(10\) is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(9\).

3. If \(r>0\) and \(10\mid r\), then
\[
D(r)<r.
\]
To see this, write \(r=10q\). Positivity of \(r\) implies \(q>0\). Appending a terminal zero does not change digit sum, so \(D(r)=D(q)\le q<10q=r\).

We now fix an arbitrary \(n>0\), and put
\[
d=D(n).
\]
By the first fact, \(0<d\le n\).

We first split off from \(d\) all prime factors that can occur in a power of \(10\). Let
\[
a=v_2(d),\qquad b=v_5(d),\qquad g=2^a5^b,
\]
and define
\[
e=\frac d g.
\]
Thus
\[
d=ge.
\]
The integer \(e\) is positive, it divides \(d\), and it has no prime factor \(2\) or \(5\). Consequently,
\[
\gcd(10,e)=1.
\]
Moreover,
\[
g\mid 10^d.
\]
Indeed, \(2^a\mid d\) and \(5^b\mid d\). In particular the exponents \(a,b\) are no larger than \(d\), so \(2^a5^b\mid 2^d5^d=10^d\). Since \(e\mid d\le n\), we also have
\[
e\le n.
\]

The next step is to choose an integer \(B\) satisfying
\[
0\le B<e
\quad\text{and}\quad
e\mid n+9B.
\]
Such a \(B\) exists because the linear congruence
\[
9B\equiv -n\pmod e
\]
is solvable exactly when \(\gcd(9,e)\mid n\). We verify this divisibility condition.

Since \(e\mid d\),
\[
\gcd(9,e)\mid \gcd(9,d).
\]
On the other hand, \(d=D(n)\equiv n\pmod 9\), so
\[
\gcd(9,d)=\gcd(9,n).
\]
Therefore
\[
\gcd(9,e)\mid \gcd(9,n)\mid n,
\]
as required.

For completeness, the solution of the congruence can be made explicit. Let \(h=\gcd(9,e)\), write \(n=hq\), and choose integers \(u,v\) satisfying Bézout's identity
\[
h=9u+ev.
\]
Then \(B_0=-uq\) satisfies
\[
n+9B_0=hq-9uq=evq,
\]
so \(e\mid n+9B_0\). Taking the least nonnegative residue of \(B_0\) modulo \(e\) gives a \(B\) with \(0\le B<e\) and the same divisibility property. Since \(B<e\le n\), we have \(B\le n\), and hence \(n-B\) is a nonnegative integer.

We next construct an integer \(C\) whose digit sum is exactly \(n\) and which is divisible by \(e\). This is the main construction.

Choose
\[
L=\max\{2,\varphi(e)\},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. We claim that
\[
10^L\equiv 1\pmod e.
\]
If \(e=1\), this is automatic. Suppose \(e>1\). Since \(\gcd(10,e)=1\), we cannot have \(e=2\). The only positive integers with totient equal to \(1\) are \(1\) and \(2\), and \(\varphi(e)>0\), so in this case \(\varphi(e)\ge2\). Therefore \(L=\varphi(e)\), and Euler's theorem gives
\[
10^L=10^{\varphi(e)}\equiv1\pmod e.
\]
In every case, \(L\ge2\).

For clarity, we describe decimal digit strings from least significant digit to most significant digit. Let \(U\) be the length-\(L\) block
\[
U=(1,0,0,\ldots,0),
\]
and let \(V\) be the length-\(L\) block
\[
V=(0,1,0,\ldots,0).
\]
Thus the integer represented by \(U\) is \(1\), the integer represented by \(V\) is \(10\), and each block has digit sum \(1\). The requirement \(L\ge2\) ensures that both blocks are well-defined.

If a length-\(L\) block of value \(x\) is repeated \(m\) times, its value is
\[
x+10^Lx+10^{2L}x+\cdots+10^{(m-1)L}x.
\]
Because \(10^L\equiv1\pmod e\), this repeated block has value congruent to \(mx\pmod e\), and its digit sum is \(m\) times the digit sum of the block.

Form a digit string \(\mathcal C\) by concatenating, in least-significant-first order,
\[
n-B\text{ copies of }U
\]
followed by
\[
B\text{ copies of }V.
\]
Every entry of \(\mathcal C\) is a valid decimal digit. Its digit sum is
\[
(n-B)\cdot1+B\cdot1=n.
\]
Let \(C\) be the integer represented by \(\mathcal C\). The first portion, consisting of the \(U\)-blocks, has value congruent to \(n-B\pmod e\). The second portion, before accounting for its position, has value congruent to \(10B\pmod e\). It begins after \((n-B)L\) digit positions, so its contribution is multiplied by \(10^{(n-B)L}\). But
\[
10^{(n-B)L}=(10^L)^{n-B}\equiv1\pmod e.
\]
Consequently,
\[
C\equiv (n-B)+10B=n+9B\equiv0\pmod e.
\]
Thus
\[
e\mid C.
\]

The digit sum of \(C\) is exactly the sum of the digits in \(\mathcal C\), namely
\[
D(C)=n.
\]
There is no issue if the most significant entries in the displayed string are zero: deleting leading zeros neither changes the represented integer nor changes the sum of its digits. Also, because the digit sum of \(\mathcal C\) is the positive number \(n\), the represented integer \(C\) is nonzero.

Now define
\[
k=10^d C.
\]
In decimal notation this appends \(d\) zeros on the right of the decimal expansion of \(C\). Hence
\[
D(k)=D(C)=n.
\]
We also have \(d\mid k\). Indeed, from the construction,
\[
d=ge,
\qquad g\mid10^d,
\qquad e\mid C.
\]
Writing \(10^d=gr\) and \(C=es\), we obtain
\[
k=10^dC=(gr)(es)=d(rs),
\]
so \(d\mid k\). Since \(d=D(n)\), this says
\[
D(n)\mid k.
\]
The other required divisibility is immediate from \(D(k)=n\):
\[
D(k)=n\mid n.
\]

It remains to check positivity and distinctness. Since \(D(k)=n>0\), we cannot have \(k=0\), whose digit sum is \(0\). Thus \(k>0\). Also \(d>0\), so \(10\mid10^d\), and hence \(10\mid k\). By the third elementary digit-sum fact,
\[
D(k)<k.
\]
If \(k=n\), then the already established identity \(D(k)=n\) would give
\[
D(k)=n=k,
\]
contradicting \(D(k)<k\). Therefore \(k\ne n\).

We have proved that for every \(n>0\) there exists a \(k\) such that
\[
k>0,
\qquad k\ne n,
\qquad D(n)\mid k,
\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
Thus the set of positive Harshad amicable partners of \(n\), distinct from \(n\), is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least element, and that least element is positive. The sequence value \(a(n)\) is precisely this least element when the partner set is nonempty, and is defined to be \(0\) only when the set is empty. Since the set is nonempty for every positive \(n\), we conclude that
\[
\boxed{a(n)\ne0\quad\text{for every }n>0.}
\]
